title: EU Gas Imports Could Reach 98% by 2050 Without New Field Investment
gist: Wood Mackenzie modeled three EU domestic gas production scenarios to 2050 and found a roughly 1,000 bcm gap between doing nothing (98% import dependency) and maximizing domestic output (38% of demand met domestically), with the outcome hinging on exploration success in the Black Sea/East Mediterranean and on fiscal and permitting reform over the next five years.

insights.claim: Without new domestic gas field investment, the EU will import over 98% of its gas by 2050, up from 85% today.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Frames a hard structural ceiling on European energy security absent policy action, a baseline against which to judge any future EU gas policy announcement.
insights.quote: Without new field investment, the EU will import over 98% of its gas by 2050.
insights.locator: central finding of a new Wood Mackenzie report

insights.claim: EU gas import dependency stays roughly flat near 85% through the early 2030s even as Norwegian supply comes off plateau, North African export volumes face domestic demand pressure, and Russian pipeline gas is phased out, because LNG fills the resulting gap.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The simultaneous decline of three legacy pipeline/LNG sources creates a structural opening that LNG suppliers, especially US exporters, are positioned to fill through the 2030s.

insights.claim: LNG's share of EU gas supply could rise from around 40% today to 63% by 2050, with the United States expected to supply 77% of that LNG.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Positions US LNG exporters and associated shipping/regasification infrastructure as the direct long-term beneficiaries of Europe's widening import gap.
insights.quote: Its share of EU supply could rise from around 40% today to 63% by 2050. Of that, 77% is expected to come from the United States.

insights.claim: In Wood Mackenzie's low-case (no new field investment) scenario, EU domestic gas production falls from 43 bcm in 2028 to just 2 bcm by 2050, with LNG covering the entire shortfall.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sets the floor case investors should treat as the default trajectory absent any policy catalyst.
insights.locator: The low case is the baseline

insights.claim: Under the mid-case scenario, reflecting current policy and investment levels, EU gas production holds near 40 bcm until 2038 (330 bcm, or 70%, more cumulative output than the low case), yet domestic gas never covers more than 17% of EU demand across the period.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Shows that even the current, business-as-usual investment trajectory leaves the EU's strategic import exposure essentially unchanged, so status-quo policy is not a hedge against import dependency.
insights.locator: The mid case reflects current policy

insights.claim: Sustaining even the mid case's ~40 bcm production plateau requires replacing more than half of the EU's currently producing gas base, meaning large new investment is needed just to avoid decline, not to gain ground.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Highlights that apparent production stability masks a high underlying reinvestment requirement, a red flag for anyone assuming flat output implies flat capex needs.
insights.quote: Sustaining today's output requires enormous investment just to stand still.

insights.claim: Only the high-case scenario, requiring stabilized fiscal terms, accelerated permitting, and resolved corporate constraints, materially changes the EU's strategic position, with production reaching 77 bcm by 2042 and meeting 38% of demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific policy levers (fiscal stability, permitting speed, resolving corporate constraints) that investors and governments should track as leading indicators of whether the high case becomes realistic.
insights.locator: The high case is the only scenario

insights.claim: Cumulative high-case EU gas output of 1,400 bcm would displace the equivalent of 615 LNG cargoes a year compared with the low case.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Quantifies how much slack could be removed from global LNG demand if the EU pursues maximal domestic development, relevant to gauging future LNG market tightness.
insights.locator: The high case is the only scenario

insights.claim: Lewis Lawrence, Wood Mackenzie's Senior Research Analyst for Europe Upstream, argues the mid case changes little for the EU's strategic position and that the real question is whether governments will create conditions for the high case, because the window for doing so is narrowing.
insights.speaker: Lewis Lawrence, Senior Research Analyst, Europe Upstream at Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A named WoodMac analyst frames the next few years as a closing window for policy action, useful as a timing signal for monitoring EU gas policy developments.
insights.quote: The mid case is often where expectations settle, but it changes very little for the EU's strategic position... The real question is whether governments are willing to create the conditions that make the high case possible, because the window is narrowing.

insights.claim: Exploration accounts for 70% (680 bcm) of the roughly 1,000 bcm gap between the low- and high-case EU gas production scenarios, making it the single largest driver of upside.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Exploration success, not incremental development of known fields, is the dominant lever for shifting the EU toward the high case, so exploration well results are the key data points to track.
insights.locator: Exploration drives most of that upside

insights.claim: The Black Sea and East Mediterranean hold 70% of the yet-to-find exploration volume behind the high case, with Greece alone accounting for a third of that potential.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Concentrates investor attention on Black Sea and East Mediterranean frontier basins, with Greece specifically as the single largest sub-region of yet-to-find upside.
insights.locator: Exploration drives most of that upside

insights.claim: Energean and ExxonMobil are preparing to drill Greece's first deepwater exploration well in 2027, a concrete near-term catalyst for whether the exploration-driven high case begins to materialize.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The 2027 Greek deepwater well is a specific, dated catalyst investors can track as an early read on the high-case exploration thesis.
insights.locator: Greece alone accounts for a third

insights.claim: Cyprus, modeled separately from the main scenarios, has a maximum re-import potential of up to 340 bcm via Egypt, a 24% uplift on the high case, though Wood Mackenzie does not expect all of that volume to reach Europe.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Adds an additional, discounted upside case via Cyprus-Egypt gas flows that investors should treat as optionality rather than a base-case assumption.

themes.theme: Cost and Emissions Case for Domestic Gas

insights.claim: US LNG delivered to northwest Europe breaks even 68% above the cost of Neptun Deep gas and 96% above the cost of new Norwegian gas.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Domestic EU gas is dramatically cheaper on a breakeven basis than imported US LNG, a strong economic argument for removing fiscal/permitting barriers to indigenous supply.
insights.quote: US LNG delivered to northwest Europe breaks even 68% above Neptun Deep gas and 96% above new Norwegian gas.

insights.claim: Domestic gas carries a fraction of the emissions intensity of imported LNG; in the Netherlands, LNG provides 50% of gas supply but accounts for 88% of overall supply emissions intensity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gives EU policymakers an emissions-based rationale, alongside the cost case, for favoring domestic gas development over LNG imports.

insights.claim: EU fiscal terms for gas investment look competitive on paper but are repeatedly undermined by instability, exemplified by the temporary solidarity contribution introduced in 2022 that remains subject to legal challenge as of 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Regulatory uncertainty, not headline fiscal terms, is flagged as the real deterrent to upstream investment in the EU.

insights.claim: EU gas policy is sharply diverging: Denmark, France and Spain have legislated end dates for gas production and closed the door to new licenses, while East Mediterranean and Black Sea nations are actively competing to attract explorers.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Investment capital and exploration activity will likely concentrate in Black Sea/East Mediterranean frontier states rather than legacy Western European gas producers, a geographic reallocation to watch.

insights.claim: The policy and investment decisions made in the next five years will determine which side of the roughly 1,000 bcm gap the EU lands on by 2050.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete near-term (2026-2031) monitoring window for EU fiscal and permitting reform as the key variable determining Europe's long-run gas import dependency.
insights.locator: The policy and investment decisions made in the next five years
